hints: Divide the derivatives and use $\sec^2\theta=1+\tan^2\theta$ to express the result only in $\tan\theta$.
walkthrough:
Differentiate the parametric equation for $x$, $x = \ln\cos\theta$, using the chain rule:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}\theta} = \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} \cdot \dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\theta}(\cos\theta) = \dfrac{-\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = -\tan\theta$$

Differentiate the parametric equation for $y$, $y = 3\theta - \tan\theta$, with respect to $\theta$:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}\theta} = 3(1) - \sec^2\theta = 3 - \sec^2\theta$$

Use the standard Pythagorean trigonometric identity $\sec^2\theta = 1 + \tan^2\theta$ to write the numerator entirely in terms of $\tan\theta$:
$$3 - \sec^2\theta = 3 - (1 + \tan^2\theta) = 3 - 1 - \tan^2\theta = 2 - \tan^2\theta$$

hints: A normal gradient of $1$ means the tangent gradient is $-1$.
Set the expression from part (i) equal to $-1$ and solve the resulting quadratic in $\tan\theta$.
Use $0\le\theta<\pi/2$ to select the valid root, then substitute that exact $\theta$ into $y=3\theta-\tan\theta$.
walkthrough:
Relate the gradient of the normal to the gradient of the tangent $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$:
$$m_{\text{normal}} = -\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{d}y/\mathrm{d}x} = 1 \implies \dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = -1$$

Set the derivative expression from part (i) equal to $-1$:
$$\dfrac{\tan^2\theta - 2}{\tan\theta} = -1$$

Factorise this quadratic in $\tan\theta$:
$$(\tan\theta + 2)(\tan\theta - 1) = 0$$
This gives two possible roots for $\tan\theta$:
$$\tan\theta = -2 \quad \text{or} \quad \tan\theta = 1$$

Apply the given domain $0 \le \theta < \dfrac{1}{2}\pi$:
In this first quadrant interval, $\tan\theta \ge 0$, so $\tan\theta = -2$ is rejected as having no valid solution.
Hence:
$$\tan\theta = 1 \implies \theta = \dfrac{1}{4}\pi$$

Substitute $\theta = \dfrac{1}{4}\pi$ into the parametric equation for $y$ to obtain the exact $y$-coordinate:
$$y = 3\theta - \tan\theta = 3\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\pi\right) - \tan\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\pi\right) = \dfrac{3\pi}{4} - 1 \quad \left(\text{or } \dfrac{3}{4}\pi - 1\right)$$
